title: Audio Lesson: Graduated Security Model
limitations: Generated from concept pages; not yet reviewed.
Content may drift from source; verify against current main.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Binary allow-or-deny security forces a bad choice: either the agent can do everything, which is dangerous, or nothing, which is useless. Graduated security gives you seven modes ranging from allow-all to deny-all, with nuanced options in between.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The seven modes are: allow-all for development, auto-approve-safe for normal work, ask-unknown as the default, ask-all for sensitive tasks, auto-deny-unsafe for high-security, deny-all for lockdown, and plan-only where the agent plans but needs approval to execute.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Bypass-immune protections are always enforced, even in allow-all mode. The dot-env file, SSH keys, slash-etc-passwd — these are never accessible regardless of the permission setting. Similarly, dangerous commands like rm-rf and drop-table always require confirmation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The evaluator is stateful. It tracks denial history. When too many operations get denied within five minutes, the mode automatically downgrades — auto-approve becomes ask-unknown, then ask-all. The system gets more restrictive when it detects repeated risky behavior.
